articles.title: Zenzap raises $44M for its AI chat app that aims to replace WhatsApp in the workplace
articles.author: Ivan Mehta
articles.content:
Many businesses around the world use consumer-facing chat apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, or iMessage to talk and coordinate with staff, and exchange documents or data.

Guy Weiss is buildingZenzap, a private messenger with AI that wants to help companies communicate with their staff and arm them with their organization’s context while staying in line with IT and security rules.

The company has raised $44 million in funding from investors including Bessemer, Lightspeed, and The Garage, as well as individual investors Wix president Nir Zohar and former GM of EY, Yoram Tietz.

The fundraise is interesting because Weiss is raising money for the first time in his career. In 2012, he bootstrapped e-commerce marketing platform StuccoMedia, and sold it to Market Group in 2015. After that, he became an investor for a few years. In 2022, he founded Zenzap after meeting Bessemer partner Adam Fisher and noodling on different ideas along with his current co-founders Noam Neumann and Jonatan Bien.

Weiss said he initially bootstrapped the app and worked out of Bessemer’s office.

“I didn’t want to raise capital. The only thing I had to lose was my name, and I was super afraid to do a second round as a founder and become a failure, because my first round was very successful. I didn’t need to work for money. So, when I met Adam, I actually started my idea with my own capital,” he told TechCrunch.

Weiss said Fisher convinced him that Zenzap should be a venture-backed business, as the company would need capital to scale.

He said that the idea was to build a messaging app for a wide range of businesses, ranging from hospitality and construction, to healthcare and fast food.

“You can’t use WhatsApp or iMessage within a workplace with the AI agent on top of it because it doesn’t comply with IT. So that’s off the table. You can’t implement Slack and Microsoft Teams because they were not built for this day-to-day use case for mobile-first that is meant for average users,” Weiss said.

Zenzap offers usual chat features on its free tier, including group chats and direct messages, task management, calendar integration, and schedule management, as well as AI-powered voice chat and search. Organizations can pay for plans starting from $51 per month for up to 20 users to unlock voice and video calls, smart task sorting, task templates, and higher limits on file storage. The paid tier also lets you use the AI search across the workspace and turn messages into tasks.

The company also offers AI agents for workflow automation as well as AI-aided voice note and call transcriptions. For these features, it has a credit-based pricing system.

At the moment, Zenzap lists organizations like FedEx, Dollar General, Taco Bell, Starbucks, Casey’s, and Regal as clients. Weiss added that branches of fast food chains like IHOP and McDonald’s often coordinate shifts and talk about supply on its platform.

“Each vertical has its own use case and workflows, which they self-serve with AI, but they all share something in common,” he said.

The startup has 50 staff in the U.S., Tel Aviv, and Europe. In the near future, the company wants to hire in its product and R&D departments.

Bessemer’s Fisher said Zenzap’s focus on catering to a broad range of people could work in its favor. He said that even the venture firm is using the messenger within its investment team to discuss and manage deal flows, showing that it can cater to different kinds of audiences.

“The only work platform with any allegiance is Slack, and that’s almost entirely among the developer community. Zenzap is not focused on developers, but on the other 99% of employees using personal messaging apps and waiting for an agent of their own. People desperately want a clear separation of work from their personal lives, and the adoption of personal and work agents makes it imperative that separation happen now,” he told TechCrunch in an emailed statement.

articles.title: Apate sends AI agents undercover to get scammed so they can gather fraud intelligence
articles.author: Ram Iyer
articles.content:
Most companies use AI agents to ship products faster or to speed up workflows.Apate.aisends them undercover to get scammed.

Founded in 2024 on the basis of research done in Macquarie University in Sydney, the Australian startup deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, sporting different ages, genders, and accents, and speak various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

The company says its fleet of agents has so far wasted 17 years of scammers’ time across 2.5 million conversations. More importantly for Apate’s customer base of banks, telecom companies, government agencies, and utilities, the undercover agents try to get scammers to reveal things about themselves that are usually learned onlyaftera victim has been scammed: bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, malicious websites, the brands they’re impersonating, and other details about the scams they’re running.

Apate, one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, then feeds that information to its customers, who use it to inform their anti-fraud measures and initiatives. (The companywill pitch a panel of VC judges at Disrupt, which is taking place this week at Moscone West in San Francisco through Thursday, October 15.)

It’s a curious evolution of scam-baiting, but it’s not so surprising given how much AI has empowered scammers and hackers. The FBIreceivedmore than 22,000 complaints of AI-related crimes in 2025, which resulted in about $893 million in losses. More than $632 million of that came from investment scams, in which the FBI says fraudsters use AI to run conversations, and deepfake the voices and appearances of celebrities, executives, and trusted figures.

For a long time, people have made a hobby out of deliberately stringing scammers along — sometimes hilariously, like getting scammers toread aloud entire books, or even toget ridiculous tattoos. Now, with AI growing increasingly capable, the tables are turning.

Curiously, the idea behind Apate was sparked by a real scam call.

Several years ago, Apate’s founder and CEO Dali Kaafar was at a family picnic when he got a call from an unknown number. Realizing it was a scammer on the line, he decided to play dumb for the benefit of his kids and managed to keep the call going for 44 minutes.

Everyone had a laugh, but Kaafar noticed that those were 44 minutes the scammer had not spent calling a real victim. It was also 44 minutes of his wasted time, which led him to wonder: Could he automate it, and in the process, learn something useful?

That idea eventually led to research work at his job at Macquarie University, where Kaafar and his colleagues used machine learning and natural language processing to uncover the content of scam calls, and develop better ways to detect and prevent scams.

“Most of the industry works after the fact. Telcos block numbers, but scammers just get new ones. Banks watch transactions, but by then the scammer has already reached the customer. We go to the scammer directly and get the information before anyone gets hurt,” Brad Joffe, co-founder and chief commercial officer, told TechCrunch. “Our AI agents talk to tens of thousands of scammers every day across calls, messages, email, and the web. What we offer our customers is what comes out of those conversations, and what they can do with it.”

Joffe said Apate uses both frontier models and its own fine-tuned models to power its agents and analysis. The company trains its models on conversations its agents have had with scammers, as well as the research Kaafar did at Macquarie.

In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get access to an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more. Customers can even assign these agents particular missions, such as obtaining a bank account number or crypto-wallet address. Its text agents can search forums, investment groups, and social platforms for potential scam activity, and can then enter conversations with a fabricated identity to surface scammers’ details.

The startup’s customers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia, TPG Telecom, as well as other utilities, telcos, and government agencies. Joffe said TPG has diverted nearly 590,000 calls to Apate’s agents, Commonwealth has seen a 76% drop in publicly reported scam losses, and an unnamed Australian bank the startup works with has used its outbound agents to disrupt 22 scam campaigns.

Investors are betting there is money to be made from fooling scammers, too. Apate raised $8.15 million in seed funding in August from Lobby Capital, OIF Ventures, Investible, Concept Ventures, and Baobab Ventures. Joffe said the 20-person company has raised just under $10 million in total and plans to spend the latest round on its product and international expansion, including opening an office in London and building a larger presence in the U.S.

“Apate is named after the Greek goddess of deception, which felt appropriate given what our agents do,” Joffe said, adding that the startup even features scammers swearing at the bots in its pitch material.

“We track that as a sign of frustration and every swear word gets celebrated by us at Apate. We are probably one of the only businesses in the world that celebrates when people swear at our product.”

articles.title: Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff amid intensifying competition for user attention
articles.author: Ram Iyer
articles.content:
Netflix is laying off about 6% of its employee base, or close to 1,000 staff, the company confirmed to TechCrunch.

The streaming giant said most of the cuts would affect its product, tech, legal, and human resources departments. The company said it will “continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas” to improve its service, and stated it is on track to deliver its full-year forecast.

Netflix had 16,000 full-time employees as of the end of last year, according to itsannual filingwith regulators.

The Wall Street Journal firstreportedthe news, citing an internal memo sent to employees.

“Our mission—to entertain the world—is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” the Journal cited the company’s co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters as writing in the memo.

The layoffs come in the wake of aprotracted bidding warfor Warner Bros. Discovery’s streaming and studio businesses that Netflix lost to Paramount Skydance earlier this year. Netflix ostensibly saw great potential in Warner Bros.’ assets, which include its studios, HBO, streaming platforms, games, and TV networks such as CNN and HGTV.

Long the dominant TV app, Netflix has in recent yearsfaced intensifying competitionfrom the likes of YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and other social apps to attract and keep users’ eyes. According to reports from various market research firms, social apps like TikTok arecatching upto Netflix when it comes to user engagement, and YouTube issaidto have surpassed Netflix in average daily viewing in 2025.

The streaming giant has been trying extensively to extract more value from its subscribers,raising prices, expanding its ad-supported tier, and investing inlive events and sports, gaming, and children’s programming to increase user engagement.

It has also bet onAI-supported features,gaming, andvideo podcasts, and has dabbled inshort-form video contentalongsideredesigning its mobile appto compete for users’ attention with social media platforms.

In 2025, Netflix reported revenue of $45.2 billion, and said ad revenue had risen to over $1.5 billion.

articles.title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
articles.author: Lauren Forristal
articles.content:
YouTube MusicannouncedWednesday the rollout of a new labeling system aimed at improving transparency around songs created with the help of generative AI. Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.

The label will appear on the player page. Clicking on this label provides additional information about the specific role of AI in the track’s creation.

Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.

YouTube said it collaborated with various music partners and deployed its own detection tools to identify AI-generated music. According to itshelp page, partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.

“Fully Gen AI” applies to tracks that are entirely generated by AI, while “Partly Gen AI” refers to works where artists may have incorporated AI-generated components but added their own live elements. Tracks edited using pitch-correction tools such as Auto-Tune fall under the “No Gen AI” category.

The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches. For instance,Apple Musichas plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year.Spotifyalso has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.

Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly90,000fully AI-generated tracks daily. The platformlabels detected AI-generated musicand excludes it from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, while also withholding royalties from fraudulent streams. The company is also working on an option to let usersfilter out AI-generated music.

TIDALalso labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.

YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions. Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization. YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its toolDream Track, which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.

articles.title: NTangible bets it can predict how athletes will perform under pressure
articles.author: Amanda Silberling
articles.content:
When collegiate sports programs recruit athletes, they can measure concrete metrics like a player’s sprint speed, throwing velocity, and physical strength. But there has never been a clear way to quantify the mental aspects of sports — how well will this athlete perform in high-pressure situations? Will they stay calm, focus, and give it their best shot? Or will they panic in the spotlight and mess up?

NTangibleco-founder and CEO Dan Connerty thinks he’s unlocked the secret to measuring if a player will execute in the most important moments.

“We really wanted to hyper focus on this idea of clutch performance,” Connerty, a professional baseball player turned sports-tech entrepreneur, told TechCrunch. “Cognitive [science] itself is just this black box that nobody’s wanted to touch, because nobody’s had the ability to measure it accurately prior.”

Alongside psychologist Dr. Ed Levine, a professor emeritus at the University of South Florida, Connerty developed a psychological assessment that he says can predict how likely an athlete is to perform under pressure. TheClutch Factorassessment is inspired by the Thematic Apperception Test, a psychological examination in which people are presented with photos of ambiguous situations and describe what they see happening, who they imagine themselves to be in the scene, and what they think might happen next.

“There’s no right or wrong answers,” Connerty said. “The key words that you use, the way in which you use those words, and the semantic phrasing associated with it get scored against the neurolinguistic scoring guide that psychologists created, and it shoots out your clutch factor score.”

The score is between 0 and 1,000 and, according to Connerty, an athlete who scores over a 750 is twice as likely to commit to a Division I school.

“What we’ve been able to do is leverage this analysis, where we can show the predictive ability,” he said. “This number can be heavily used in rankings, leaderboards, recruiting conversations, NIL conversations, and scholarship conversations, especially in the crazy wild west that is collegiate sports right now, where we’re writing $4 million checks to quarterbacks.”

A possible flaw in the product, however, could be that athletes seeking to impress coaches and recruiters may answer the questions dishonestly to get a higher clutch score. When I took the quiz and answered honestly, I got a below-average score of 584, which didn’t surprise me — I dreaded high-leverage situations when I played high school sports. When I took the quiz a second time, answering as I imagined a very level-headed, clutch, top recruit might respond, I scored 802.

Perhaps the platform would work better as a way for coaches to learn more about their athletes and help them improve in weaker areas. Connerty thinks that “clutch” is a skill that can be trained. While he isn’t positioning NTangible as a training platform, he worked with former MLB sports psychologist Howie Schwartz to create a list of exercises that athletes can use as a starting point for upping their mental game.

While Connerty’s background is in baseball, NTangible now supports testing for nine sports. He also has ambitions to expand the clutch test to apply to corporate settings, so that HR departments can evaluate employees’ strengths and weaknesses under pressure. TheNTerpretassessment translates more directly to the workplace — the respondent answers questions about how they best respond to coaching and feedback, giving management data on how that employee processes instructions and acts on information.

NTangible’s most viable business model seems to be selling to sports organizations and companies directly, rather than to individual athletes. The company will elaborate on its strategy onstage on Wednesday at TechCrunch Disrupt, where it’s currently among the top 20 companies dueling for the grand prize at Startup Battlefield.

You can check out the rest of the field, and the investors who will decide the winner, byjoining us in person this weekat Disrupt, happening Tuesday through Thursday, October 13 to 15, in downtown San Francisco.

But there has never been a clear way to quantify the mental aspects of sports — how well will this athlete perform in high-pressure situations?

articles.title: Scimplify raises $25M to challenge China’s grip on critical materials with AI
articles.author: Jagmeet Singh
articles.content:
As manufacturers across industries strive to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers, Indian startupScimplifyhas raised $25 million to expand its AI-powered approach to producing specialty chemicals and critical materials, with semiconductors, defense, and energy emerging as key growth markets.

The all-equity strategic round was led by Hitachi Ventures, with customers Henkel and Teknor Apex joining as new investors. Existing backers Accel India, Bertelsmann India Investments, Omnivore, and 3one4 Capital also participated. The round values the Bengaluru-based startup at $250 million after the investment, according to a person familiar with the transaction, up from$150 millionafter a $40 million Series B round in March 2025. The latest investment brings Scimplify’s total equity funding to $80 million, the startup said, though it declined to disclose its valuation.

The growing adoption of AI and advanced computational tools has accelerated materials discovery and research. However, turning promising chemistry into commercially available products at scale remains a slow and complex process. Manufacturers need to develop production processes, qualify facilities, and meet stringent quality standards, all while navigating supply chains limited to a handful of countries. Scimplify is seeking to shorten that process.

In some cases, the startup, founded in 2023, has gone from receiving a customer’s requirements to delivering the finished material in just two months, compared with the 12 to 18 months such work would typically take, co-founder Sachin Santhosh (pictured above) said in an interview.

Once it receives an order, Scimplify develops chemical manufacturing processes at its research facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad and then transfers them to partner factories for commercial production. Its proprietary AI platform, Scinode, helps coordinate the work by identifying suitable production routes and manufacturing facilities, while tracking quality and regulatory requirements. The platform uses specialized AI agents for different functions, including research, manufacturing, and quality control, Santhosh told TechCrunch.

“Each of these agents is basically solving for what [a customer] would want, working backward from the customer’s requirement,” Santhosh said. “This helps us move a lot faster and remember customer context even for future references.”

Scimplify’s in-house team of scientists and engineers oversees production across a network of more than 500 manufacturing facilities. It helps customers establish alternative sources for materials whose supply is concentrated in China and a few other countries.

About 90% of Scimplify’s manufacturing currently takes place in India. The startup, however, plans to expand its production network to the U.S. and Japan over the next year as it seeks to attract more customers in both markets, Santhosh said.

The U.S. has emerged as a key growth market, with Scimplify’s annualized revenue run rate in the country rising sixfold to about $60 million from $10 million a year ago, according to Santhosh. The market now accounts for roughly 30% of its business, while customers outside India collectively contribute more than half of its revenue, compared with less than 5% about 18 months ago.

Overall, Scimplify, which serves more than 1,000 customers and has delivered products to more than 40 countries, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $200 million, tripling from a year earlier, Santhosh told TechCrunch. The startup is targeting a $400 million annualized revenue run rate over the next year. Scimplify has also been EBITDA-positive for the past two months and expects to turn profitable after tax this month, he said.

Energy, electronics, and defense now account for about 45% to 50% of Scimplify’s revenue, up from less than 15% a year ago, Santhosh stated. The growth comes as AI fuels demand for materials used in electronics and energy infrastructure, while ongoing wars drive demand from the defense industry.

Scimplify is working on producing tungsten derivatives from scrap, offering customers an alternative source of materials whose supply is heavily concentrated in China. The startup is also working on rare-earth materials, another category where global supply chains remain heavily dependent on China.

The startup works with customers including Japanese electronics manufacturer TDK, German chemicals group BASF, and Hitachi. Santhosh cited a project involving TDK as an example of how the startup can shorten the time needed to develop and deliver specialty materials. Timelines, he said, vary depending on the project.

With its latest funding, Scimplify plans to deploy around $7.5 million for its U.S. expansion, including building out its manufacturing network, Santhosh said, adding that the allocation could change as the startup’s plans evolve. It also earmarked another $2 million for further development of Scinode.

The startup employs about 340 people, including roughly 70 scientists. Most of its workforce is based in India, though it also has local teams in the U.S., Japan, Indonesia, and the UAE.

articles.title: The founder’s guide to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Everything you need to know
articles.author: TechCrunch Events
articles.content:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era? Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that, based on the feedback we’ve gotten from the community and the reality on the ground. And everything kicks off in just a few days,act now before your chance to save $100 on your pass comes to an end.

Last year at Disrupt, we spoke with founders about their experiences and discovered the results of their attendance firsthand. One founder saw a 3x oversubscription rate after their confirmation forStartup Battlefieldand more than 100 investor inbounds helping fuel conversations about a future fundraising round. Another founder had nearly 30 back-to-back conversations with investors who flocked to them after a pitch onstage and followed them to theirbooth.

That’s not the exception at Disrupt — that’s the point. And those opportunities aren’t just available for Battlefield finalists. Every conversation in theExpo Hallor in aSide Eventcan create an opportunity for your startup. For years, whether it’s been held in New York, San Francisco, or elsewhere, Disrupt has brought together thousands of founders, investors, startup team members, and tech leaders.

We’re keeping that mission alive at SF’s Moscone West, this October 13-15with a packed lineup of speakers, more than 200 expert sessions, a wealth of organized and serendipitous networking opportunities, and most of all, the chance to be in the same room as the person who could change your nascent idea for a company or your current startup’s trajectory.

This guide is for the founders out there who are just learning about Disrupt, who need a refresher, or are skeptical of whether it’s worth it. TechCrunch has been around for more than 20 years; we can take it. And before you dive in, we have two discounts that run up until Disrupt begins you should be know about.Founders can bring a team member along for 50% off their ticket by following this link, or you can help laid off members of your networkfind their next opportunity at Disrupt with our steep discount of Expo+ passes.

If you’re asking Claude or ChatGPT if TechCrunch Disrupt is worth it, you’re not alone. The reality is that Disrupt is a unique event, and it’s happening at a unique time for the startup community.

This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it. Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology.

Whether you’re raising your first round, scaling your team, or deciding how AI changes your product, every session is designed to answer one question: “What can I take back to my company on Monday morning?”

Disrupt works a bit differently, depending on where you are in your founding journey, with different tracks you can follow to make the most of the three days:

You’re here to pressure-test your thesis, meet your first angel or pre-seed investors, and figure out who else is building in your space.Prioritize the Builders Stage, the Startup Battlefield semifinalist pitches, and the Expo Hall, along with roundtables tied to your industry and conversations you’ll want to learn more from.

You’re here for capital and validation above all else, and your time is valuable. Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app. You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors.

And when your schedule isn’t packed with dealmaking, learn from VC perspectives and fundraising-focused sessions at theBuilders Stage.

You’re here in search of talent, strategic partners, and market visibility. Those same networking tools and opportunities can help you meet potential hires and partners and deepen those connections or make new ones.Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed— there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find.

The Startup Battlefield winner’s reveal packs the Disrupt stageand is each year’s capstone event. But it’s the lead-up to that $100,000 check and the deluge of attention the winner receives that’s the most valuable for founders attending Disrupt.

The 200 startups chosen on August 20 to compete go through a rigorous prep process and get the opportunity to pitch onstage in front of top-tier VCs and the Disrupt crowds. You’ll also get to watch those pitches, take notes, learn from the peaks and valleys, and potentially meet the teams behind the ideas and innovations. It could be in a follow-up meeting or just walking through the halls of Moscone.

And if that all leaves you inspired, here’s an insider tip: Most Battlefield participants, and several winners, have gone through the process multiple times. We’re no longer taking applications for 2026’s competition, but we’reexpandingtheprogramtomore internationalmarkets, and the 2027 process will besimilar to this year’s, so take note for the future!

Disrupt 2026 spans several stages, each built around a different founder need:

And that’s just the beginning — we’ll have more speakers to announce as we get closer to Disrupt.Check out the full lineup of speakers across all stages and events here.

Disrupt’s prices increase as we get closer to the event, but we have a couple of promotions for Founders looking to save.You can save 50% on a second ticket by following the link here, and bring a coworker or co-founder along for the ride.

If there are colleagues in your network who have been impacted by layoffs who you’d like to have join up, we have an option for them as well, witha special $75 Expo+ Pass available at a limited volume for those impacted by cutbacks this year.

Your time at Disrupt is valuable, too, so before you head there, check on ourregularly updated schedule of speakersandSide Events, get ahead of competitors’ schedules by booking your networking opportunities in advance, and get your own elevator pitches in order to make the most of those magical Disrupt moments that can come at any point October 13-15!
